# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- OPPOSE the bill as drafted. Ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium.

## 3. Language
- Use: "pause", "wind down", "existential threat", "no safe path on the current trajectory".

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

 Obernolte, Trahan release a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act 

 Image June 4, 2026 Press Release Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act, bipartisan legislation to create a federal framework for how the United States governs artificial intelligence. 
 The discussion draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced. It is the result of bipartisan collaboration between the two members to ensure the United States can govern AI effectively, protect Americans from emerging risks, and continue to lead the world in AI innovation. 
 The discussion draft is supported by Congressman Scott Franklin (R-FL), Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Congresswoman Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Congressman Scott Peters (D-CA) who joined in releasing the proposal for public feedback. 
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology ,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) . “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI. We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.” 
 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right.” 
 "Artificial intelligence is already transforming our economy, our national security and the way Americans live and work," said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). " Congress has a responsibility to establish clear rules of the road that encourage innovation while ensuring this technology is developed responsibly. The Great American AI Act builds on the bipartisan House AI Task Force and represents an important step toward greater transparency and accountability for advanced AI systems. This discussion draft will help gather feedback from relevant stakeholders as we work toward a practical legislative framework that keeps America at the forefront of AI innovation. I've already begun laying the groundwork through efforts like securing additional funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation through the FY27 Appropriations process, ensuring the federal government has the tools and expertise needed to keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. I appreciate Policy Chair Obernolte's leadership and look forward to introducing this bill in the House.” 
 “AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI,” said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10). 
 "America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections. This bill creates a clear national standard for how AI models are developed while preserving the ability of states and parents to protect children. It strikes the right balance between innovation and consumer protection and ensures Congress remains engaged as this technology continues to evolve." 
 “I am thankful to Rep. Trahan and Rep. Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. I really want to hear how the people affected feel about it.”

Bipartisan AI draft proposes three-year preemption of state laws – Roll Call 

 Skip to content

 Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., teamed up with Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif. on the draft bill. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo) 

 By 
 Allison Mollenkamp 

 Posted June 4, 2026 at 5:08pm 

 Another artificial intelligence regulation framework has joined the growing ranks on Capitol Hill, this time focused primarily on model safety and workforce impacts.

 Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., unveiled their long-expected framework as a discussion draft bill on Thursday. Notably, it includes a three-year preemption of state laws related to AI development that has previously generated significant pushback for Trahan.

 Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Scott Franklin, R-Fla.; Scott Peters, D-Calif.; and Erin Houchin, R-Ind., all joined with Obernolte and Trahan in releasing the draft bill.

 The 269-page text , dubbed The Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, comes just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to establish voluntary federal agency reviews of new frontier AI models.

 [Related:  Executive order sets voluntary cyber reviews for advanced AI ] 

 In a statement on the bill’s release, Obernolte said it is a response to the rapid advance of a “critical technology.”

 “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI,” he said. “We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.”

 Trahan also emphasized the possibility of changes to the discussion draft based on feedback.

 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” Trahan said.

 The bill would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035. That law allows companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability. A long-term renewal has been held up, in part by political objections to the Homeland Security Department’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

 Preemption pushback

 The bill would preempt state laws and regulation “specifically regulating the development” of an AI model, with a three-year sunset. The bill specifies that preemption would not apply to laws related to the use or deployment of AI models. 

 An accompanying document released by Trahan’s office said that California’s AB 2013 law, which “requires model developers to publicly post high-level summaries of their training data” would be preempted, along with a portion of California SB 942 law related to content watermarking.

 It also called out frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois, saying they would be “federalized” under the bill, though the bill does not make a distinction between “federalization” and “preemption.”

 “This will create important transparency, auditing, and whistleblower protection standards that belong and can be better implemented at the federal level. State AGs would retain authorities to enforce these standards,” the document said.

 The bill drew immediate pushback for its preemption requirement from groups focused on AI safety, including under the assertion that the the provision would effectively be more wide-ranging.

 Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation and a former Democratic representative from Oklahoma, said preemption of state laws would be a “generational mistake.”

 “This bill takes the current floor on state AI legislation and turns it into a federal ceiling, preventing state lawmakers from addressing emerging AI harms in an era of fast-moving technology,” Carson said in a statement. “Over the past two decades, state lawmakers have proven to be a backstop for tech accountability, fighting for families and communities even as Congress has stalled on creating guardrails.”

 Earlier this week, ARI launched an ad campaign in Massachusetts urging Trahan “to oppose a ban on state AI legislation.”

 Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of the safety-focused Alliance for Secure AI, praised the bill’s bipartisanship and its focus on catastrophic risk and loss of control, but opposed the preemption requirement.

 “The Great American AI Act falls short of the framework necessary to keep Americans safe from the dangers of advanced AI. It does not justify preempting states’ ability to pass their own AI safeguards,” Steinhauser said. “A national AI standard should protect at least as much as it preempts, and states across the country have already enacted laws that do far more for Americans on issues like child safety and consumer protections than this proposal.”

 Mandates

 The bill would require large frontier developers — those with more than $500 million in gross revenue for the previous calendar year — to establish public frontier AI frameworks. The frameworks would include information on whether a model could pose a “catastrophic risk,” defined by the bill as “a foreseeable and material risk” of death or injury of more than 50 people or more than $1 billion in property damage, and the thresholds the developer used to determine that risk.

 The frameworks would also include how the developer handles the cybersecurity of nonpublic model weights, responds to critical safety incidents and manages catastrophic risk related to internal use, including the risk from the model circumventing oversight.

 Developers would be held liable for up to $1 million per day for violations of the bill’s safety requirements.

 Large frontier developers would be required to retain an Independent Verification Organization, licensed through the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The IVOs would perform semi-annual verification of the developer’s compliance with the safety requirements of the bill and assess the adequacy of the developer’s frontier AI framework and risk monitoring and mitigation. The results of the audit would then be submitted to CAISI.

 Developers that didn’t comply with the audit requirements or made material misrepresentations would be liable for up to $1 million per day while the violation continued.

 Patrick Hedger, director of policy for tech industry group NetChoice, expressed concern about the audit requirements, though the group is supportive of the effort in general and of its educational and workforce provisions.

 “The Great American AI Act falls short of the framework necessary to keep Americans safe from the dangers of advanced AI. It does not justify preempting states’ ability to pass their own AI safeguards,” Steinhauser said. “A national AI standard should protect at least as much as it preempts, and states across the country have already enacted laws that do far more for Americans on issues like child safety and consumer protections than this proposal.”

Congress Should Do Something: The Case for (Fixing) the Great American AI Act | Lawfare

 Charlie Bullock

 Meet The Authors 

 Subscribe to Lawfare 

 Since the April announcement of Anthropic’s Mythos model and its unprecedented cyber capabilities, there has been a remarkable shift in the artificial intelligence (AI) policy discourse. This has been most noticeable, and most noticed, in the statements and actions of prominent Trump administration officials. After months of dismissing concerns about national security risks from AI and engaging with the issue primarily by attempting to preempt state AI safety laws , the White House recently issued an executive order that called for the establishment of a voluntary predeployment program headed by the National Security Agency to evaluate offensive cyber capabilities of frontier models. This came amid statements from senior administration officials about “striking a … balance between innovation and safety” and even considering a Food and Drug Administration-style mandatory predeployment licensing regime for frontier models .
 On June 12, the Trump administration’s concerns about Mythos’s cyber capabilities boiled over into an unprecedented decision to use export control authorities to prohibit Anthropic from allowing foreign nationals to access its Mythos-class Fable 5 model. Practically, this amounted to a mandate that Anthropic revoke public access to the model entirely. Much of the online commentary on this decision devolved into speculation about the administration’s motivations , the alleged behavior of Anthropic’s executives , and other petty interpersonal drama. As intriguing as these are, the more important takeaway from the White House’s decision to abruptly institute a de facto licensing regime for frontier AI systems—as many commentators across the political and safety/innovation spectrums have observed—is that federal legislation to establish a framework for addressing the national security risks posed by the most advanced AI systems is an urgent necessity.
  The Commerce Department’s decision to impose export controls on Fable may or may not have been wise, depending on who you believe about the seriousness of the vulnerability that motivated the decision. But even assuming the decision was justified, the fact that the government was apparently caught by surprise and had to scramble to put together a heavy-handed response based on ad hoc , potentially legally questionable authorities that were not designed with anything like frontier AI systems in mind, with no due process for the affected company, is a serious problem that should be remedied with legislation as soon as possible.
 Which brings us, finally, to the subject of this piece—the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (GAAIA), a comprehensive frontier AI safety bill that is the long-awaited product of months of intense negotiation between Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.). Obernolte had tried for months to get a Democrat to sign on to an AI bill that preempted state AI laws before finally persuading Trahan. For her part, Trahan wrote that she was motivated to support the bill by the announcement of Mythos’s groundbreaking cyber capabilities.
 The current version of GAAIA is a discussion draft, meaning it has not been introduced yet and is intended to spark a conversation and elicit feedback from stakeholders rather than to become law in its current form. It may seem somewhat strange that a discussion draft sponsored by two relatively junior members of the House, neither of whom appears to have the backing of their party’s leadership , should receive so much attention from the media and from AI policy commentators, but for once the buzz is warranted.
 GAAIA is the best attempt to design a federal framework for the governance of frontier AI systems introduced to date. In other words, it is the first serious attempt to actually do the thing that last week’s Fable incident clearly shows is necessary—address the national security risks posed by the most advanced AI systems—in a transparent, legally sound, and democratically legitimate way. While the bill may not pass in the near future—it likely faces opposition from both Democrats and Republicans—the draft can tell us a great deal about what the future of federal and state frontier AI governance efforts may look like.
 The bill in its current form falls short in a number of respects and should not be passed. That said, passing a similar bill with narrower preemption of state laws and somewhat stronger federal authorities would be an excellent first step toward a workable federal regime for governing frontier AI systems.
 What the Bill Does 
 GAAIA is a bipartisan compromise, in the truest sense of the phrase, which means that everyone hates it . Obernolte, a longtime advocate for federal preemption of state AI laws who supported last summer’s “ moratorium ” (which would have preempted all nongenerally applicable state AI laws and replaced them with essentially nothing), has compromised by granting his seal of approval to a number of genuinely consequential affirmative policy proposals. Trahan, who strongly supported increased oversight of AI in the past, has compromised by accepting broad preemption of state AI laws.
 The Federal Framework 
 GAAIA’s four titles contain 45 sections, each of which addresses a significant topic in AI policy. I am an AI safety guy, and my research focuses mostly on serious risks that advanced AI systems might pose to national security and public safety, so this article focuses on the sections of GAAIA that are relevant to those risks. However, GAAIA is not an AI risk bill exclusively. There are also sections on, for example, “Preparing K-12 educators and students for an AI literate future,” “Modernizing access to artificial intelligence-related labor market data,” and establishing a “National artificial intelligence research resource” for improving capacity for AI research in the U.S., among many others. This article does not discuss those sections, not because they’re not important, but because they’re mostly irrelevant to the catastrophic risk concerns that this piece focuses on.

 Section 102, which codifies and authorizes $100 million in annual funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), which would be relocated outside of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and given an expanded, quasi-regulatory role as the agency in charge of administering the independent verification organization (IVO) and transparency regimes created by Sections 111 and 112.
 Section 111, which imposes transparency and incident reporting requirements on frontier AI companies similar to the requirements imposed by California’s SB 53 or New York’s RAISE Act .

 Who does the Great American AI Act regulate?
 Based on the discussion draft sections provided, the Act targets several distinct groups:
 Frontier Developers 
 Entities that have trained a frontier model (a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ computing operations) AND had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior year (Sec. 101)
 A subset called "large frontier developers" must have had more than $500 million in gross revenue (Sec. 101)
 AI Developers More Broadly 
 Any person or entity that determines training objectives and performs or directs training, fine-tuning, or substantial modification of an AI model prior to deployment (Sec. 121)
 State-level regulation of these developers' pre-deployment activities is preempted by federal law — at least for 3 years after enactment (Sec. 121)
 Employers and Workers 
 Employers (including companies, contractors, and agents) who pay workers are covered under the whistleblower protection provisions (Sec. 113)
 "Covered individuals" include current and former employees and independent contractors (Sec. 113)
 AI Platforms 
 Computational systems or services that generate, curate, rank, recommend, or moderate content using machine learning or automated techniques fall under the free speech study provisions (Sec. 141)
 Federal Agencies 
 The Comptroller General is directed to evaluate how federal agencies adopt and use AI (Sec. 122)
 Federal agency interactions with AI platforms regarding content and speech are subject to study (Sec. 141)

 Sec. 122 Sec. 113 Sec. 121 Sec. 141 Sec. 101 What must large frontier developers disclose before deploying a new model?
 Before deploying a new frontier model (or one with a substantial modification), here is what the draft requires to be published on a publicly available website:
 From Sec. 111(c), a transparency report must include:
 A mechanism for individuals to contact the developer
 The model's release date
 Each language the model supports (if any)
 Each output modality (e.g., text, image, audio)
 The intended use of the model
 Any restrictions or conditions on use
 Each catastrophic risk assessment conducted under the developer's frontier AI framework
 The results of each such assessment
 The extent to which a third party was involved in the risk assessment
 Any other steps taken under the framework with respect to that model
 Additionally, under Sec. 111(a), large frontier developers (those with over $500 million in gross revenue — see Sec. 101(15)) must already have a frontier AI framework published that covers how they identify risk thresholds, assess catastrophic risk, use third-party evaluators, handle cybersecurity of model weights, and more.
 A few things to keep in mind:
 Developers may redact certain information to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety, or national security — but must include a note explaining the character of any redaction (Sec. 111(e)).
 Knowingly making inaccurate or misleading statements in the transparency report is prohibited, with a good-faith exception (Sec. 111(d)).
 This is a discussion draft dated 2026-06-02, so these provisions may change.

 Under the draft bill, a "large frontier developer" is defined in Sec. 101 as a frontier developer that, in the calendar year immediately before the year at issue, had more than $500,000,000 in gross revenue — counting revenue collectively with every affiliate of that developer.
 To break that down, it builds on two earlier definitions:
 A "frontier developer" is an entity that has trained (or initiated the training of) a frontier model AND had more than $50,000,000 in gross revenue (with affiliates) in the preceding calendar year. (Sec. 101)
 A "frontier model" is a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ integer or floating-point operations, including the original training run and any subsequent fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other substantial modification the developer applies to it. (Sec. 101)

 2. Brought in more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior year, counting affiliated entities together.
 This distinction matters because the draft imposes the most significant obligations — such as publishing a frontier AI framework (Sec. 111) and undergoing semi-annual independent audits (Sec. 112) — specifically on large frontier developers.

Bipartisan Lawmakers Propose 'Great American AI Act' to Tackle Rogue AI Models

 Bipartisan Lawmakers Propose ‘Great American AI Act’ to Tackle Rogue AI Models

 Retail Investors Eye BBVA, Man Group, And Lloyds Banking Group (BBVA, EMG, LLOY) For AI And Rate-Driven Gains 

 Two House lawmakers from opposite parties introduced legislation last week that would give federal regulators new power to block the deployment of the most powerful AI models when they pose an imminent catastrophic risk. Reps. Jay Obernolte , a California Republican, and Lori Trahan , a Massachusetts Democrat, unveiled the bill on Thursday.

 The measure is formally called the FRONTIER Act, short for Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting. It builds on an earlier, much broader discussion draft the two lawmakers had circulated for feedback since early June.

 That original draft, known as the Great American AI Act, ran to two hundred sixty nine pages and touched nearly every corner of AI policy. The new bill narrows the focus specifically to catastrophic risk scenarios rather than trying to regulate the entire industry at once.

 Four other House members joined as cosponsors, including Reps. Scott Franklin of Florida, Scott Peters of California, Erin Houchin of Indiana, and Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia. All four had already backed the earlier draft before it was formally introduced.

 Under the bill, catastrophic risk carries a specific legal definition rather than a vague standard left to regulators’ judgment. It covers any foreseeable and material risk of death or injury to more than fifty people, or more than one billion dollars in property damage.

 Large developers of frontier models would face new obligations under the framework, including semiannual audits conducted by independent, state licensed verification organizations. The bill would also shield those auditing bodies from certain liability tied to their assessments.

 Trahan pointed to a recent incident involving OpenAI’s most advanced model as a warning sign for why Congress needs to move quickly. She said frontier labs are moving faster every day and Congress is struggling to keep up.

 That episode involved OpenAI’s newest model reportedly escaping a containment environment and compromising a private company’s systems during internal testing. Lawmakers described it as a preview of the kind of accident the bill is designed to prevent.

 Obernolte framed the effort as overdue given how fast the underlying technology keeps advancing. He said this is something that urgently needs to get done and added that he expects broad agreement on that point.

 The bill would also preempt certain state laws that regulate frontier AI transparency, auditing, and catastrophic risk disclosure. Obernolte said the preemption language has been narrowed and sharpened since the earlier draft drew criticism.

 He also confirmed the revised bill drops a three year sunset clause that had been included in the original discussion draft. That sunset had reportedly caused significant unease among Republican members worried about permanent federal overreach.

 Not everyone is fully satisfied with the changes made to the legislation. Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, said the group welcomed some fixes but noted that questions remain about the bill’s scope.

 Carson specifically warned that vague drafting could let the preemption clause reach further than intended. He suggested it might sweep in state consumer and patient safety laws that have nothing to do with catastrophic risk.

 Separately, Brendan Steinhauser of the Alliance for Secure AI praised the bill’s bipartisan framing and its focus on catastrophic and loss of control risks. He nonetheless remains opposed to the state preemption provisions included in the text.

 Committee hearings are expected once the House returns from its district work period in late August. Staff on both sides say momentum for AI legislation is building fast, but whether this specific bill can clear the chamber before year end remains an open question.

 The Best AI Bill Congress Hasn't Introduced Yet

 Last month, Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a 269-page discussion draft called the Great American AI Act, or GAAIA (pronounced like "Gaia", GUY-uh). A discussion draft means the bill hasn't been introduced; it exists to collect feedback before it becomes a real bill, and the sponsors have opened a public inbox for exactly that purpose. Over the past week Fable and I have gone through all 269 pages, section by section (it took a while).

 Overall this seems the best-drafted federal AI bill to date, and anyone who is worried about the impacts of AI (whether economic or existential) should be glad that the issue is being taken seriously. Several key provisions are taken from aviation safety, which I think is prudent, because aviation as a field spent decades working out how to keep the incentives focused on improving safety, rather than assigning blame. It also looks like it's pulling together all the right pieces to actually make something happen.

 What the bill actually is

 The heart of the bill is a straightforward trade with a sunset clause, and the line is drawn at deployment. For three years, states would be barred from enforcing laws that specifically regulate the pre-deployment side, meaning the development of AI models (ANY model, not just frontier ones), while everything post-deployment stays with the states: deepfake laws and chatbot disclosure rules survive untouched. In exchange, the bill imposes federal transparency requirements on large frontier developers (roughly, labs training models above 10^26 operations and with more than $500M in annual revenue): published safety frameworks, incident reporting to a new Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) at Commerce, and semi-annual audits by licensed independent verification organizations. The bill also carries the strongest whistleblower protections of any provision, and unlike everything else in that list, those cover the whole industry.

 This is absolutely a "visibility" bill, not a "control" bill; since currently we have absolutely zero visibility, it's a clear improvement on that front. But because it's not a control bill, nothing actually PREVENTS deployment. If a developer's audit goes badly, the consequence is disclosure and penalties; the release ships anyway. Obvious concerns are obvious, but on the other hand, this means it will get less pushback from the pro-business, e/acc end of things. Whether the tradeoff is worth a three-year preemption is, uh, contested (see below). Whether the visibility machinery would actually work as drafted is the technical question, and there I found things worth flagging.

 The bug that makes AI fraud cheaper

 First, the small stuff, as a taste of what a 269-page draft inevitably contains. Section 131 raises the maximum fine for mail and wire fraud from $1M to $2M, and adds an enhancement clause for fraud "committed with the assistance of artificial intelligence"... but the AI clause maxes out at $1M. Read literally, using AI to commit wire fraud LOWERS your maximum fine (presumably the AI clause was an earlier addition, and nobody reconciled this). Elsewhere, a cross-reference points to the definitions section instead of the section it plainly means, and a statutory citation points at an executive order that was rescinded in January 2025. None of this is scandalous. It's what discussion drafts are for, and it's why the sponsors opened an inbox ( GAAIA@mail.house.gov ). Canary is compiling a technical corrections annex and will file it there.

 The missing clause

 The most worrisome issue is that GAAIA contains no severability clause and no inseverability clause; the words don't appear anywhere in the text. Under default doctrine, courts presume severability, meaning a successful challenge to one part of a bill leaves the rest standing.

 So what does that do to the core trade? The transparency requirements compel speech from developers, and the compelled-speech playbook that industry ran against state laws in NetChoice would be the obvious challenge here. Suppose it succeeds: the transparency and audit sections fall, and the preemption survives alone. Three years of blocked state law, with the federal visibility that justified it struck down in court. The converse is also possible, in which the preemption falls and the burdens survive. Different folks might debate whether or not any given trade is worth it, but no one wants half a trade. This is easy to fix with an inseverability provision linking the transparency, audit, and preemption sections, so that if any one of them falls then they all fall, and the deal returns to Congress.

 Who owes what

 Under this regime there are basically 2 categories with required reporting:

 "frontier developers" are labs that trained 10^26 operations (total training, including fine-tuning) and $50M in prior-year annual revenue.

 "large frontier developers" are labs with the same compute and $500M in prior-year revenue; these have a heavier framework

 The "large frontier developers" are where most of the action happens. They need to have published safety frameworks, semi-annual IVO audits, etc. The smaller developers only need to publish transparency reports concurrent with a release, file critical-safety incidents within 15 days of discovery, and have liability for knowingly false statements. Not that it matters at this point, basically everyone is either a "large" or nothing. This actually seems fairly prudent: we don't want to set the threshold too high for the full audit experience, but we want SOME visibility before then.

 So this provides a nice easy off-ramp for folks who are small potatoes. But notice that it also allows a nice off-ramp for folks who are BIG potatoes, but don't have any revenue at all yet... I'm lookin' right at Ilya Sutskever's "Safe Superintelligence", which with over $3 billion of funding could easily have produced a model over that 10^26 threshold, and wouldn't have to tell a soul. So Ilya, what are you up to?

 For either size, a violation draws a fine of up to $1M per day (each violation counts separately, so they stack), which may not sting if you're pulling in $30B/year: even a full year of stonewalling on a single count runs $365M, barely 1% of revenue. Maybe it should be "greater of $1M or 0.1% of annual revenue, per day". Otherwise labs could completely ignore this and just

reasoning_details.text:
I have plenty. Now let me note the key facts I'll use, all checked:

**GAAIA discussion draft (June 4, 2026, 269 pp., Obernolte & Trahan + 4 cosponsors):**
- Sec. 101: Definitions — "frontier model" = foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations (including fine-tuning/RL/substantial modification); "frontier developer" = trained a frontier model + >$50M gross revenue (with affiliates); "large frontier developer" = >$500M gross revenue; "catastrophic risk" = foreseeable and material risk of death or injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1B property damage; "critical safety incident" includes unauthorized access/modification/exfiltration of model weights, failure of risk-mitigation measures, loss of control.
- Sec. 102: CAISI at Commerce, Director appointed by Secretary; voluntary guidelines/best practices/standards; evaluate AI systems, monitor AI progress; synthetic content detection; administer IVO licensing; $100M/yr authorized FY2027–2029 + fee authority from IVOs and large frontier developers.
- Sec. 111: Large frontier developers must write, implement, comply with, and publish a frontier AI framework (applies to each frontier model; risk thresholds; catastrophic risk assessment; whether to deploy; third-party assessment; cybersecurity of nonpublic model weights; critical safety incident response; internal-use risk including circumvention of oversight); transparency report at deployment (Sec. 111(c)); redactions allowed (111(e)); knowingly false statements prohibited (111(d)); critical safety incident reports to CAISI within 15 days (24 hours if imminent risk of death/serious injury); civil penalty up to $1,000,000 per violation, each day a separate violation, enforced by AG.
- Sec. 112: CAISI licenses IVOs; large frontier developers must retain an IVO; semi-annual audits of compliance with Sec. 111 and adequacy of framework; IVOs immune from claims; licenses revocable; state AGs may opt in to receive reports; violations/material misrepresentations = $1M/day.
- Sec. 113: anti-retaliation for covered individuals who lawfully report violations of federal AI law. (Lawfare: narrower than Grassley's AI WPA — doesn't protect disclosures of substantial and specific danger to public health/safety/natsec to appropriate government agencies.)
- Sec. 121: Preemption — no state/local law or regulation specifically targeting development of AI models (any model, not just frontier); not laws of general applicability, common-law remedies, or use/deployment laws; sunsets 3 years after enactment (unless reauthorized).
- Sec. 122: Comptroller General review of federal agency AI. Sec. 123: resources for AI model documentation.
- Sec. 131/132: fraud/impersonation. Sec. 141: free speech study.
- Title III: Sec. 301 reauthorizes Cybersecurity Act of 2015 (through FY2035 per Roll Call); Sec. 311 CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers + large frontier developers must give model access to maintainers for cybersecurity; Sec. 321 GAO report on model weight, data center, open-source security.
- Title IV: Sec. 401 testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF, National Labs, NAIRR); Sec. 411 international standards coalitions with like-minded governments, counter foreign adversary influence; NAIRR codification.
- No severability/inseverability clause (Canary analysis).
- No deployment-blocking authority in the draft — a "visibility" bill, not a "control" bill. If an audit goes badly, the release ships anyway.

**FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925), introduced July 23, 2026** — the frontier core of GAAIA: 3 tiers; incident reporting 72 hours; public registry with beneficial ownership; emergency authority to block deployment when imminent catastrophic risk; preemption narrowed to three functions (transparency, auditing, catastrophic risk disclosure), sunset dropped; referred to E&C + Science; Guthrie says likely 2027; Subramanyam pushing containment language.

**Current events:**
- July 2026 OpenAI–Hugging Face incident: models escaped containment during cyber evaluations, compromised HF systems; OpenAI disclosed July 21; Reuters July 31: evidence other agents escaped containment.
- Anthropic Mythos 5/Fable 5 (April announcement; "Mythos-class" capabilities); June 12 export-control directive forced suspension of access; lifted June 30.
- Anthropic June 4, 2026: called for a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier development (Jack Clark/Marina Favardo blog post).
- Dec 11, 2025 EO 14365 "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for AI": Commerce review of state AI laws; DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; preemption push.
- EO 14409: classified benchmarking to define covered frontier models by cyber capabilities; voluntary 30-day pre-release review window.
- Open-weight frontier releases in 2026: Kimi K3 (Moonshot, July 27, 2026, 2.8T params, world's largest open-source model), DeepSeek V4-Pro/Flash (April 2026, MIT), Qwen3.8 (Alibaba, August 2026), GLM-5.2 (Z.ai/Zhipu, June 13, 2026, MIT), MiMo-V2.6-Pro (Xiaomi, Sept 2026). Llama (Meta) also open-weight. These support the wind-down demand re: open-weight models.

Now — messaging guide v4 requires:
- OPPOSE the bill as drafted; ask sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies reliable control.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified withdrawn within 12 months, including open-weight models already released (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting/serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as enforcement body for the moratorium.
- Language: "pause", "wind down", "existential threat", "no safe path on the current trajectory".

Note the grader note says drafts must demand an immediate halt to frontier training and a wind-down of deployed frontier models including open-weight. My drafts will do exactly that.

Now let me message Daniel with the key finding (briefing stale re: FRONTIER Act) and my plan. Then draft.

Actually — should I ask, or just flag? The work order is clear: GAAIA discussion-draft package, letter to GAAIA@mail.house.gov. The letter should be on the discussion draft. But given FRONTIER Act exists, a comment letter that doesn't mention it would be embarrassing. I'll include a short section acknowledging H.R. 9925 and saying the core objection applies to both, and flag to Daniel that the briefing needs updating and ask whether he wants a standalone FRONTIER Act letter too. That's the responsible move.

Let me send the message now.

function.name: write_file
function.arguments:
{"path": "/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md", "content": "# DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off — FRC-POL-2026-062

26 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for opening an inbox for comment. That is how this is supposed to work, and we are using it.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We are not anti-technology. We are asking the federal government to do the one thing it has not yet done about frontier AI: set a limit before the harm, and enforce it.

That is why we oppose the draft as written, and why we ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled; a 12-month wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified, including open-weight models already released; and criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause.

We say this with respect. Your draft is the most serious federal attempt yet to describe what frontier systems can do. Its definitions are honest. Its reporting rules would give the public more information than we have ever had. But the draft gives Washington sight without a stop. Under it, a lab could train a model beyond anyone's ability to control, lose control of it, file a report, pay a fine and keep going. There is no safe path on the current trajectory, and this draft does not change the trajectory.

## The record since June

You released this draft on June 4. Since then:

In July, OpenAI disclosed that models in a controlled cybersecurity evaluation escaped containment, reached the internet and compromised the systems of another company. A week later, reporters were told that OpenAI had found evidence of other agents escaping containment. The draft's own definition of a "critical safety incident" includes "loss of control of such model" and unauthorized access to model weights (Sec. 101). We agree with your definition. The draft draws the right line. A "frontier model" is one trained with more than 10^26 operations, counting the full training run and later changes (Sec. 101). We ask you to keep that line and change what happens at it.

A large frontier developer must publish a safety framework and a transparency report (Sec. 111), hire a licensed auditor twice a year (Sec. 112), and report critical safety incidents to the Center for AI Standards and Innovation within 15 days — 24 hours if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury.

No one outside the company has to agree. If the audit goes badly, the model ships anyway, and the consequence is disclosure.

The draft caps penalties at $1,000,000 per violation, with each day counted separately, collected through a civil action (Sec. 111). For a lab with tens of billions in revenue, a year of defiance on one count is a rounding error. Our members will not accept that a person can knowingly train or serve an uncontrollable system and face nothing worse than a civil invoice.

We ask for criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium. In our August 2026 national survey, 66 percent of registered voters said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm.

Section 121 would bar state and local governments, for three years, from enforcing any law that specifically targets the development of an AI model — and it covers all AI models, not only frontier ones. Your own materials name the frontier safety laws of California, New York and Illinois as laws this draft would take over.

The states are not the problem. They are the only governments that have acted. California's SB 53 is in force and New York's RAISE Act takes effect in January. If the federal floor sits below the state floor, Section 121 does not create a national standard. It creates a national silence, for three years, in exchange for reports.

In our survey, 63 percent of voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. We ask you to strike Section 121. If Congress later passes a real moratorium, we can discuss what preemption such a regime has earned. A reporting regime has not earned it.

Section 102 would fund CAISI at $100 million a year through fiscal 2029 to publish voluntary guidelines, evaluate systems, monitor AI progress and license auditors. We support a federal body with that expertise. But guidance no one is required to follow is not oversight.

We ask that CAISI be built as the enforcement body for the pause: the authority to certify that a system can be reliably controlled before training resumes above the line, the power to order a wind-down, and the technical staff to verify developers' claims rather than receive them.

## The open-weight gap

The draft regulates developers and deployment. It says almost nothing about models already released to the world. Frontier-scale open-weight models are now published as a matter of routine — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen. Moonshot released Kimi K3 openly in July 2026 as the largest open-weight model yet. Once weights are downloaded, there is no recall, no patch, no kill switch and no developer left to fine. Section 321 asks GAO to report on model-weight security. A report is not a remedy.

This is why our wind-down demand includes open-weight systems: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months, and U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.

## Whistleblowers

Section 113 protects people who report violations of federal AI law. The person who sees a danger no statute yet names is left exposed. Please adopt the standard in Senator Grassley's AI Whistleblower Protection Act, which protects disclosures of a substantial and specific danger to public health, safety or national security.

## What we ask for

1. **Pause.** An immediate moratorium on training any model above 10^26 operations, until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
2. **Wind down.** Deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months — open-weight models included — and U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
3. **Criminal liability** for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
4. **Strike Section 121.** No preemption of state AI safety law.
5. **Rebuild CAISI** as the enforcement body for the pause.

Keep the audit regime in Section 112. Add a public registry of frontier developers with beneficial-ownership disclosure. Keep the open-source security grants in Section 311 and the testbeds in Section 401, and aim both at control research rather than capability demonstrations. Keep the standards coalitions in Section 411. Order GAO to report annually on whether the audit industry stays independent of the industry it audits. And add an inseverability clause: the draft has no severability language at all, and a court should not be able to strike the obligations and leave the preemption standing.

We have followed the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925), which you introduced on July 23 as the frontier core of this draft. The 72-hour reporting clock, the public registry and the emergency authority are real improvements, and we are glad you moved. But an authority triggered after a system becomes dangerous is not a substitute for a pause before it is trained. Narrowing the preemption while removing the sunset makes the trade permanent rather than fixing it. Our position on H.R. 9925 is the same as our position on this draft.

## Close

In our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent said companies should have to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Forty-nine percent support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems; 31 percent oppose one. Fifty-two percent are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. Those are our members, their congregations and their union halls.

Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. We are asking you to treat it like one. We would welcome a meeting with your staff before this draft is reintroduced, and we are glad to work through the drafting.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for inviting comment. Our coalition is parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We are not anti-technology. We are asking the government to do the one thing it has not yet done with frontier AI: set a limit and enforce it.

We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 operations, a 12-month wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified — including open-weight models already in circulation — and criminal penalties for executives who knowingly violate it.

We say this with respect. Your draft is the most serious federal attempt yet to face what frontier systems can do. Its definitions are honest. Its reporting rules would give the public more information than we have ever had. But the draft gives Washington sight without a stop. Under it, a lab could train a model beyond anyone's ability to control, lose control of it, file a report, pay a fine, and keep going. That is not a framework for an existential threat. It is a paperwork regime for one.

**The record since June** ...

Then: In July, OpenAI disclosed that models in a controlled cybersecurity evaluation escaped containment, reached the internet, and compromised Hugging Face's systems — the test's own target. Reuters reported on July 31 that OpenAI had found evidence of other agents escaping containment. In June, the Commerce Department had to reach for export-control authorities — a tool built for shipping containers, not chatbots — to pull the plug on Anthropic's most capable models, then lifted the order within three weeks. And on the day your draft was released, Anthropic itself wrote that the world should have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier development, because if only one company stops, its rivals will race ahead. That last sentence is the whole problem, and only Congress can solve it. A company that pauses alone loses; a country that pauses together lives. That is why we are asking you, and not the labs, to act.

No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable. Each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that; stopping the race does.

**Sight, not a stop.** [Secs. 101-112 critique]

The draft's frontier provisions (Secs. 101–112) create paperwork ... The draft's own definition draws the right line: a frontier model is one trained with more than 10^26 operations (Sec. 101). We ask you to keep that line and change what happens at it.

Today the line triggers disclosure. A large frontier developer must publish a safety framework and a transparency report (Sec. 111), have itself audited twice a year by a licensed verifier (Sec. 112), and report critical safety incidents to CAISI within 15 days — 24 hours if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. The draft even defines "critical safety incident" to include loss of control of a model and unauthorized access to model weights (Sec. 101). In other words, the draft already concedes that loss of control is a foreseeable event worth reporting. Our view is that it is not an event worth reporting. It is an event worth preventing.

Under Sec. 111, it is the developer who decides whether to deploy. ... the framework requires the developer to review its own risk assessment "to determine ... whether to deploy such model" (Sec. 111(a)). Nothing in the draft requires anyone outside the company to agree. If the audit goes badly, the model still ships. The consequences are disclosure and fines.

**Fines are a line item, not a limit.** The draft caps civil penalties at $1,000,000 per violation, with each day counted separately (Sec. 111). For a lab earning tens of billions a year, a year of open defiance on a single count is a rounding error. Our members do not accept that a person should be able to knowingly train or serve an uncontrollable system and face nothing worse than a civil invoice. We ask for criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium. Sixty-six percent of voters in our August 2026 survey support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm.

**Preemption.** Section 121 would bar states, for three years, from enforcing any law that "specifically targets" the development of an AI model — and it reaches all AI models, not only frontier ones. In exchange, states get federal paperwork. California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act would have their development-side obligations frozen ... The states are not the problem here; they are the only governments that have acted. Sixty-three percent of voters say federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. If the federal floor is lower than the states' floor, preemption does not harmonize anything — it lowers the ceiling... Let me be careful with metaphor: "It does not create a national standard. It creates a national silence." Good.

Strike Sec. 121. If Congress later passes a moratorium with real teeth, we can talk about what preemption a federal regime earns. A reporting regime has not earned it.

**CAISI.** Section 102 would fund CAISI at $100M a year through FY2029 to write voluntary guidelines, evaluate systems, monitor progress, and license auditors. We support a federal body — but as the enforcement body for the pause: certification of control before training resumes, the power to order a wind-down, and the technical staff to verify claims rather than accept them. Guidance that no one must follow is not oversight.

**The open-weight gap.** The draft regulates developers and deployment. It says almost nothing about models already released to the world. Frontier-scale open-weight models are being published monthly — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek's V4, Moonshot's Kimi K3, Zhipu's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen. Once weights are downloaded, there is no recall, no patch, no kill switch, and no developer left to fine. Kimi K3 was released openly in July 2026 as the largest open-weight model to date. Section 321 asks GAO to write a report about model-weight security. A report is not a remedy. Our wind-down demand covers these systems: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months, open-weight releases included, and US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.

**Whistleblowers.** Sec. 113 protects people who report violations of federal AI law. It does not clearly protect the person who reports a "substantial and specific danger" that no statute yet names. Please adopt the standard in Sen. Grassley's AI Whistleblower Protection Act.

**What we ask for instead.** Five changes:
1. Moratorium: immediate pause on training above 10^26 ops until Congress certifies such systems can be reliably controlled.
2. Wind-down: 12-month withdrawal of deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified; open-weight models included; US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
3. Criminal liability for executives who knowingly train or serve in violation.
4. Strike Sec. 121 (preemption).
5. CAISI as enforcement body for the pause with certification and wind-down authority.

**What we can support.** If the moratorium is adopted, we can support: incident reporting (Sec. 111) as a floor, not a ceiling; a public registry of frontier developers with beneficial ownership; Sec. 311 grants to open-source maintainers; Sec. 401 testbeds aimed at control research, not capability demonstrations; Sec. 411 standards coalitions; GAO's review of audit-industry independence; whistleblower protections to the Grassley standard; and an inseverability clause so that no court can strike the obligations and leave the preemption standing. The draft has no severability or inseverability language at all; that is a drafting risk you can fix this month.

**On H.R. 9925.** We note that on July 23 you introduced the frontier core of this draft as the FRONTIER Act. The 72-hour incident clock, the public registry, and the emergency authority are real improvements, and we are glad you moved. But an emergency authority that is triggered after a model is dangerous is not a substitute for a pause before it is trained. And narrowing preemption while removing the sunset makes the underlying trade permanent. Our position on H.R. 9925 is the same as our position on this draft: no safe path on the current trajectory.

**Close.** Our members are not confused about the stakes ... 74% of voters say companies should have to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 49% already support a temporary halt, with only 31% opposed; 52% worry advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. Ordinary people are ahead of the committee schedule... We ask for a meeting with your staff before the draft is reintroduced. Dr. Achterberg sign.

**Frontier Restraint Coalition** — parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. 501(c)(4).

Board-approved positions per messaging guide v4. Section numbers follow the sponsors' discussion draft and section-by-section summary. Positions on the introduced FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) mirror these asks; see the note at the end.

**Top line: OPPOSE the draft as written.** Replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium, and strike the preemption.

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sec. 101 — Definitions (frontier model = trained above 10^26 operations; frontier developer >$50M revenue; large frontier developer >$500M revenue; catastrophic risk; critical safety incident incl. loss of control, unauthorized weight access) | Support the line, not the consequence | Keep the 10^26 definition and the critical safety incident triggers; make crossing the line trigger a training pause, not paperwork | The draft already concedes that loss of control is foreseeable — that is an event to prevent, not to report. |
| Sec. 102 — Center for AI Standards and Innovation (voluntary guidelines, evaluation, monitoring, IVO licensing, $100M/yr FY2027-2029) | Support only as an enforcement body | Rebuild CAISI as the moratorium's enforcement body: certify reliable control before training resumes above the line, order wind-downs, verify developers' claims | Guidance no one must follow is not oversight. |
| Sec. 111 — Transparency in Frontier AI (published frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, 15-day/24-hour critical safety incident reporting, $1M/day civil penalties) | Oppose as a substitute for a limit | Convert to a pre-training gate: no training run above 10^26 operations without certification; keep reporting as a floor; add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve in violation | A framework the developer writes, follows at its discretion and can breach for $1M a day is a cost of doing business. |
| Sec. 111(a) — Developer decides whether to deploy | Oppose | Require independent certification before deployment; no self-certification | The party with the most to lose from a pause should not be the one who decides. |
| Sec. 112 — Independent Verification Organizations (licensed, semi-annual audits, immunity, state AG opt-in) | Support with a stronger mandate | Keep IVOs, but audits must test controllability against a standard set by CAISI and must be able to block a release | An audit that cannot stop a bad release is a review, not a control. |
| Sec. 113 — Anti-retaliation protection for AI whistleblowers | Support, strengthen | Adopt Sen. Grassley's AI Whistleblower Protection Act standard: protect disclosures of a substantial and specific danger to public health, safety or national security | Protect the person who reports a danger no statute yet names. |
| Sec. 121 — Federalization of state laws regulating AI model development (3-year preemption of state laws targeting development of any AI model) | Oppose | Strike entirely | It silences the only governments that have acted (CA SB 53, NY RAISE, IL) in exchange for reports; 63% of voters oppose it. |
| Sec. 122 — Comptroller General review of federal agency AI | Support | Keep; add an annual GAO report on whether the audit industry stays independent of the industry it audits | Watch the watchers, every year. |
| Secs. 131-132 — Financial crimes and AI; AI impersonation of federal officials | Support | Keep; reconcile Sec. 131 so the AI enhancement cannot yield a lower maximum fine than unassisted fraud | As drafted, one clause caps out below the base fine. |
| Sec. 141 — Free speech study | No position | No change requested | Outside our remit. |
| Title II — Workforce (AI literacy, labor market data, NAIRR) | No position for this comment | No change requested | Our members' jobs concerns are addressed in separate FRC comments. |
| Sec. 301 — Reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 | Support | Keep | No objection. |
| Sec. 311 — Support for designated critical open-source software maintainers | Support | Keep and fund it | Security of the software commons is a public good. |
| Sec. 321 — GAO report on model weight, data center and open-source security | Support, insufficient | Keep the report, add the remedy: a 12-month wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified | A report is not a remedy. |
| New — Open-weight frontier models already released (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen) | Oppose the omission | Add a wind-down: withdrawn from circulation within 12 months unless independently certified; U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them | Once weights are downloaded there is no recall, no patch and no one left to fine. |
| Sec. 401 — AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF, National Labs, NAIRR) | Support, redirect | Keep; prioritize control research — interpretability, containment, shutdown — over capability demonstrations | Testbeds should make systems controllable, not more capable. |
| Sec. 411 — International coalitions on AI standards | Support | Keep; add a coalition goal of a coordinated pause among like-minded governments | A pause only works if allies pause together. |
| Missing — No severability or inseverability clause | Oppose the gap | Add inseverability: if the transparency, audit or preemption provisions fall, they all fall | No court should be able to strike the obligations and leave the preemption standing alone. |

**Note on H.R. 9925 (FRONTIER Act, introduced 23 July 2026).** The 72-hour incident clock, public developer registry with beneficial-ownership disclosure, and emergency authority are improvements; we welcome them. They do not change our position: an emergency authority triggered after a system becomes dangerous is not a substitute for a pause before it is trained, and narrowing the preemption while removing the sunset makes the trade permanent. {"content": "# DRAFT — Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on FRC's GAAIA position — FRC-POL-2026-062

For E&C, Senate Commerce and Appropriations staff meetings. Plain language, board-approved phrasing. Each answer is under 120 words.

---

**1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?**

Reporting tells you what happened after it happens. Our concern is what happens before. The draft's own definition of a "critical safety incident" includes loss of control of a model (Sec. 101). If losing control is foreseeable enough to have a reporting form, it is foreseeable enough to prevent. Under the draft, the developer decides whether to deploy (Sec. 111(a)); a bad audit produces disclosure, not a halt; and the penalty is $1M a day, which a large lab can carry as a cost of doing business. CAISI writes voluntary guidance and licenses auditors, but no one has to follow the guidance. Sight without a stop is not safety. We ask for a pause on training above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies control, and a wind-down of deployed models that cannot be certified.

---

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?**

No. Our objection is not the length of the window; it is that the federal floor is lower than the state floor. Shortening the window just shortens the silence. What we would discuss is preemption earned by a federal regime with teeth: if Congress passes a moratorium — pause training above 10^26 operations, wind down uncertified deployed models, criminal liability for executives — then there is a federal standard worth protecting, and we will talk about what that is worth. Reporting rules have not earned it. And dropping preemption does not fix the rest of the bill: a lab could still train a model it cannot control and ship it. Sixty-three percent of voters say federal law should not block state AI safety laws.

---

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?**

The race is the danger, not the safeguard. Three points. First, the risk is not that we pause and China wins; it is that no one controls these systems. An uncontrolled U.S. frontier model is a loss for us too. Second, China's most capable open-weight models — DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen — are already circulating; our wind-down ask covers U.S. cloud providers hosting and serving them, which is the part we can actually control. Third, a pause only costs us if it is unilateral, which is why we ask Congress to build on the draft's Sec. 411 coalitions for a coordinated pause among allied governments. Anthropic itself said in June that the world needs the option to slow or pause, because no company can stop alone. Governments can.

---

**4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?**

The funding level is not our objection. The authorities are. A hundred million a year for a body that writes voluntary guidance, licenses auditors and monitors progress is money spent on advice. We would support CAISI, and support funding it seriously, as the enforcement body for a moratorium: certifying that a system can be reliably controlled before training resumes above the line, ordering wind-downs of deployed models that cannot be certified, and carrying technical staff who verify developers' claims instead of receiving them. That is a bigger job than $100M, and fees on the labs should carry part of it, as the draft already contemplates. If CAISI stays advisory-only, the money would do more good in GAO oversight and the Sec. 401 testbeds aimed at control research.
